subject: Science
central_question: Why can carbon form an enormous variety of stable compounds, and how do their structures explain their properties, reactions and everyday uses?
in_scope_units: Covalent bonding through sharing of electrons and the tetravalency of carbon
Single, double and triple covalent bonds in simple molecules
Properties of covalent compounds and allotropes of carbon
Catenation and the versatile nature of carbon
Straight chains, branched chains, rings, structural isomers and hydrocarbons
Homologous series and basic nomenclature of carbon compounds
Combustion, oxidation, addition and substitution reactions
Properties and reactions of ethanoic acid, esterification and saponification
Cleaning action of soaps, micelles, hard water and detergents
banned_topics: Detailed petroleum refining and fractional distillation
Polymers not discussed in the chapter
Biochemistry of carbohydrates, proteins and nucleic acids

known_pitfalls.claim: Carbon normally forms C4+ or C4- ions to complete its octet.
known_pitfalls.correction: Gaining or losing four electrons is energetically difficult; carbon completes its outer shell mainly by sharing electrons and forming covalent bonds.

known_pitfalls.claim: All carbon compounds conduct electricity because carbon is present.
known_pitfalls.correction: Most covalent carbon compounds are poor conductors because electron sharing does not produce mobile ions. Graphite is an important allotrope that conducts electricity.

known_pitfalls.claim: Compounds with the same molecular formula must have the same structure.
known_pitfalls.correction: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different carbon skeletons or structures, as shown for butane.

known_pitfalls.claim: Soap works equally well in hard and soft water.
known_pitfalls.correction: Soap forms an insoluble curdy precipitate with calcium and magnesium ions in hard water, while detergents remain effective.

known_pitfalls.claim: Mustard or vegetable oil becomes healthier when hydrogenated.
known_pitfalls.correction: The chapter explains that hydrogenation converts unsaturated oils into saturated fats and notes that saturated fatty acids are considered harmful for health.

recommended_example_progression: Use NCERT Figures 4.1-4.5 and Exercise Question 4 to construct electron-dot structures and explain covalent bonding.
Use NCERT Figures 4.6-4.10 and Activity 4.2 to build chains, recognise saturation, identify isomers and form homologous series.
Use NCERT Activities 4.3-4.5 and the chemical-property questions to reason from flame, soot and colour change to combustion and oxidation.
Use NCERT Activities 4.6-4.9 to compare ethanol and ethanoic acid and explain esterification, saponification and carbonate reactions.
Use NCERT Activities 4.10-4.12 and Exercise Questions 8, 10 and 15 to explain micelles, hard-water scum and detergent action.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The NCERT end-of-chapter EXERCISES contain Questions 1-15, followed by group activities on molecular models and soap preparation.
